items.text: McDonald's is finally bringing back an iconic menu item from the 00s
items.article: McDonald's has confirmed a discontinued fan-favourite is finally returning to the UK menu after a decade and it'll cost just £1.99. From the Chicken Legend to the Breakfast Bagel, McDonald’s customers have spent years begging for discontinued menu items to come back. More often than not, their prayers go unanswered, but occasionally the fast food chain delivers. In 2024, McDonald’s revived the McRib , and now another iconic item is set to return. It’s good news for those who’ve been craving a Snack Wrap, as Metro can exclusively confirm that the cheap treat is rejoining the UK menu in just a few days. The Snack Wrap officially returns to McDonald’s UK from 11am on Tuesday, October 6. The fan-favourite was a staple on the fast food chain’s UK menu between 2006 and 2016, and featured one Chicken Select, lettuce, cheese , and cool mayo inside a flour tortilla.

Not being able to order a favourite comfort meal or give in to an impulse craving can leave regulars missing the familiar spot. That's the current sentiment amongst Mumbaikars, as one of the city's most iconic and oldest bakeries, Yazdani Bakery, has closed its doors. The place, famous for its fresh breads, brun maska, mawa cake, biscuits and more, has officially shared on its Instagram handle that it is closing for renovations. "For generations, you've made Yazdani part of Mumbai's story. Now, it's our turn to give something back. The Yazdani Bakery will be closed for renovations from September 29. Thank you for loving us and refusing us to fade. See you on the other side," the post read. items.key: ai:why carmel is racing to trim or remove 1,000 trees
items.text: Why Carmel is racing to trim or remove 1,000 trees
items.article: In tree-obsessed Carmel, more than 1,000 trees need attention prior to this winter's El Niño storms. There is arguably no city in California, or maybe even the nation, more protective of its trees than Carmel. But in the run-up to what portends to be a historic El Niño winter, a massive effort is underway in Carmel to identify trees that are unhealthy, dying or dead. They could pose a threat to the town’s citizenry and infrastructure as a super El Niño winter season grows near. Tree life in Carmel is highly valued and even has a special commission that provides oversight to the town’s 10,000-tree canopy. Mayor Dale Byrne told SFGATE earlier this month that he estimates more than 1,000 trees “need to be cut down or trimmed extensively” in the run-up to the winter months. PG&E is spearheading the effort and will complete the lion’s share of the work, according to the mayor. The mayor himself said he has been impacted by the work and explained in one circumstance that he received short notice about work that would affect a historic tree on his property. “I found out they’re going to take the telephone pole and take part of my oak tree, and I didn’t get noticed,” he said.

items.key: ai:only 6% of marketers say ai is paying off in a big way. here's what the winners are doing.
items.text: Only 6% of marketers say AI is paying off in a big way. Here's what the winners are doing.
items.article: New research from Bain, shared exclusively with CMO Insider, finds most marketers are still waiting to see the impact of their AI investments. Marketers have gone all in on AI . Now comes the awkward question: Is it actually paying off yet? The answer is largely "no," according to new research from the management consulting firm Bain, shared exclusively with CMO Insider. The starkest finding from the study, which surveyed 1,397 senior marketing and finance executives: Only 6% of marketing organizations said AI is delivering significant performance impact today. That's despite 95% of marketers saying their organizations have adopted AI tools . "It just speaks to the fact that transformation is hard, and it takes time," Laura Beaudin, a partner at Bain, told me. There's a twist, though: Companies that Bain considers "leaders" were much more likely to say they'd seen growth from AI. Bain defines "leaders" as companies with more than 11% annual revenue growth and more than 7% annual market share growth. It calls companies with flat or declining revenue or market share "laggards."

items.key: ai:delhi turned up to vote for fat dogs irl. here's what we saw at a 'polling booth'
items.text: Delhi turned up to vote for Fat Dogs IRL. Here's what we saw at a 'polling booth'
items.article: Delhi residents turned up at voting booths for the Fat Dogs of Delhi finale after the Instagram contest went offline. The event became both a community hangout and a fresh debate over care, visibility and canine obesity. “Googoo for the win!” “Team Gola always!” These were the chants in the air as Delhi went to polls on September 30. From a two-year-old exercising her power to cast a vote to senior citizens showing up at the booths, this was an election nobody imagined in their wildest dreams. After all, the candidates were not humans but four-legged tail-waggers, aka “man’s best friend” — the doggos. The viral Fat Dogs of Delhi contest reached its final leg yesterday—polling day—when people from across the capital turned up to vote for their favourite fat dog. While online voting through Instagram Stories was, of course, an option, the team also set up four physical polling stations across different parts of Delhi, giving voters the chance to cast their ballots in person. We visited one such station: Aku's burger shop in South Delhi's Vasant Vihar market. For anyone living under a rock, Fat Dogs of Delhi started as an Instagram page featuring some of Delhi’s chunkiest neighbourhood dogs and eventually turned into a full-blown electoral contest, complete with 64 contenders, multiple rounds of voting and, finally, physical polling booths. Voters wrote the name of their chosen candidate on a sticky note and got a star sticker in place of an inked finger.

items.text: 'My son accused me of eating his bread - but the truth was absolutely horrifying'
items.article: Dylan Richardson was left flummoxed when holes kept appearing in loaves of bread at his family home in Maidstone, Kent. A mother and son were left scratching their heads when large holes kept appearing in loaves of bread – and horrified to learn rats were responsible. Dylan Richardson returned to his family home in Maidstone for the university summer break, and bought a loaf as his mum Karen doesn’t normally keep bread in the house. But when the 20-year-old went to make himself a slice of toast, he discovered the bottom of the loaf had been torn open and large chunks of the bread were missing. Karen Richardson, 47, said her son accused her of eating a hole in the middle of it. When she told him she had not touched it, they wondered whether something might have happened to it before they bought it. ‘We kind of thought it was the supermarket ’s fault,’ Karen said. items.article: NBC News took a road trip along I-80, hitting some of the most competitive congressional districts to find out what’s driving people’s votes in the midterms. By Jonathan Allen, Frank Thorp V, and Marshall Crook September 29, 2026 Americans are frustrated with the direction the country is headed as the midterm elections approach — an atmosphere that typically blows up on the party in power. They’re angry about rising prices, ballooning interest rates and foreign wars. They are afraid that AI will automate many jobs while driving up utility prices. The perspectives were shared with three NBC News reporters during a six-day, eight-stop August road trip in a minivan along Interstate 80. This “Drive to Decision Day” covered one-third of the most closely contested House races in the nation and two key Senate races. The aim was to find out what Americans are most concerned about right now and how that might affect their votes in November. Keep scrolling and watch this NBC News Reports documentary to find out. So from New Jersey to Nebraska, through the Rust Belt and into America’s breadbasket, we talked to voters in longtime battlegrounds, places made more competitive by national trends or redistricting, and seats where the incumbents’ personal lives have become political challenges.
